extracted.intended_audience: public relations practitioners, PR managers, and students learning broadcast and speech communication techniques
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on producing and evaluating television/videotape messages and preparing and delivering speeches for public relations purposes, including technical, strategic, and evaluation criteria.

rubrics_metrics.name: Electronic editing preference
rubrics_metrics.description: Editing of taped video material can be accomplished with splices, but the preferred system is electronic editing, where various sounds, scenes, and images, including superimposed titles, are assembled electronically by moving each piece of recorded material from the reel on which it was shot and stored to a master finished reel, which can be duplicated for distribution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use electronic editing to assemble scenes, sounds, and titles into a master finished reel suitable for duplication and distribution rather than relying on physical splices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of sound mixers and single-track management
rubrics_metrics.description: Sound mixers enable background music, separately recorded narration, and other effects to be joined on the single sound track found on standard videotape.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plan sound layers (music, narration, effects) and mix them appropriately to fit the single track; anticipate balancing and timing during editing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Microphone selection and configuration
rubrics_metrics.description: The standard camera-recorder outfit sold by most video manufacturers includes a unidirectional microphone, with a lavaliere cord to hang it around a speaker’s neck or a simple mounting stand to hold it in place on a table. It is also useful to obtain other microphones, including an omnidirectional one for recording general sounds, crowd noise, or multiple speakers. For recordings of panel discussions or meetings, it is wise to provide all speakers with their own mikes, all jacked into a microphone switcher—a device that enables several sound sources to be picked up by the sound track on a single recorder.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Match microphone type to needs: use lavalier/unidirectional mikes for single speakers, omnidirectional for ambient/crowd sound, and a microphone switcher for multi-speaker events to ensure each voice is captured cleanly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lighting for small-format video
rubrics_metrics.description: Most video crews carry one or two light-weight sources of illumination—high-intensity lamps with reflectors, mounted on slender tripods or clamp-on devices—so that they can wipe out shadows, provide good general illumination, and 'key' on the faces of speakers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use portable high-intensity lamps with reflectors to eliminate shadows and key faces; exotic equipment is not required but basic lighting control is essential for credible video.

rubrics_metrics.name: Playback equipment and audience sizing
rubrics_metrics.description: To show video to a small audience, your organization needs a suitcase-sized playback unit that accepts the reel or cassette, and 2 standard television set or monitor equipped with an input jack. For audiences of more than ten, you can link several monitors together with cables so that no one person sits more than ten feet from a screen, or you can use special optical equipment that enlarges the image and throws it up on a movie screen for viewing by large audiences of as many as 100.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose playback format and display method appropriate to audience size (portable monitors for small groups, linked monitors for medium groups, projection for large audiences); prefer glass-screen monitors for brighter, better-focused images.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess whether television/videotape justifies cost
rubrics_metrics.description: Television commands huge national audiences for network programs, and large community audiences for local programs. Videotapes can add the glamour of television to internal communication. The question is: Do the huge audiences and the visual impact justify the cost? Frequently, the target public for a public relations program won't be in the television audience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether visual impact and audience size align with target publics before committing resources; do not assume TV is the solution for every PR problem.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of television by PR models
rubrics_metrics.description: Like radio, television can be an effective technique for each of the four models of public relations: press agents/publicists sandwich messages into entertainment and news programs; public-information specialists prepare TV handouts, place specialists on talk shows, prepare documentaries and PSAs; two-way asymmetric communicators use paid advocacy advertisements; two-way symmetric practitioners use talk shows and news specials to learn consequences and promote dialogue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose TV strategies aligned with your PR model (informational placement, paid ads, advocacy, dialogue); be aware of reactive vs proactive uses across models.

rubrics_metrics.name: Realistic objectives for television
rubrics_metrics.description: Many public relations practitioners believe television messages have great impact upon cognitions, attitudes, and behaviors. It's easy, however, to overestimate the effect of television. People retain very little of what they see and hear on television, unless they hear it over and over again. Television news introduces issues to the public agenda but stays with issues for a shorter time than print. Television commercials must be repeated many times before people remember them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Set realistic objectives for TV: primarily communication and agenda-setting; expect weak lasting effects on attitudes/behavior unless messages are repeated; plan for frequency and reinforcement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Calculate cost per thousand of target public
rubrics_metrics.description: If the audience is large the cost per thousand of a television message may be relatively small. Again, however, if you want a meaningful comparison with other media, remember to calculate the cost per thousand of your target public that sees the message on television—not of the total television audience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When budgeting, compute cost per thousand specifically for the target public reached, not the total viewers, to compare media effectiveness accurately.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use formative and evaluative research for TV decisions
rubrics_metrics.description: With television, it is essential that you use the money and time budget techniques outlined in Chapter 8. It also is imperative that you do formative and evaluative research to determine whether the effect of the television message merits the cost.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conduct pre-testing (formative) and post-broadcast evaluation to decide if television is cost-effective for your objectives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitations of ratings and need for target surveys
rubrics_metrics.description: Numerous rating services provide data that can be used to measure the communicative objective — the number of people seeing a televised message. If you can get demographic information on the viewers of a particular program, you also may be able to match characteristics of viewers with those of your target public. But remember that members of target publics do not necessarily have common demographic characteristics. Thus, the ratings often do not provide the data you need. To perform an adequate evaluation, you will need to survey members of your target public shortly after your message appears on television.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use ratings for reach estimates but always survey your target public directly after the airing to determine recall and message effects; supplement ratings with targeted research.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recommended post-broadcast survey questions
rubrics_metrics.description: Ask survey respondents if they remember seeing your message: 'Did you happen to hear a message about TRW on television last night?' If yes: 'Can you tell me what you remember about that message?' (Follow-up) 'Anything else?'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use simple recall and open-ended follow-up questions shortly after broadcast; if assessing attitude/behavioral change, use previously discussed measurement techniques.

rubrics_metrics.name: Television reaches low-involvement publics
rubrics_metrics.description: Television effects are relatively weak because television reaches primarily low-involvement publics. The audience does not seek out the PR messages; they process them passively. Even employee and community publics seldom seek out videotapes prepared by public relations people. Usually the tapes are shown as part of some other event or exhibit and receive only partial attention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect passive processing and low retention; design messages accordingly (simple, repeated, emotionally engaging) and reinforce with other channels.

rubrics_metrics.name: Count and measure viewership attributes
rubrics_metrics.description: To measure whether communication took place you might count the number of people who see the televised message and, if possible, get demographic information to match viewers to target publics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Collect reach and demographic metrics as a first step, but validate with target-specific surveys for true evaluation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adequate planning must precede speechmaking
rubrics_metrics.description: The moral of the story is that: 1. Adequate planning must precede speech-making. 2. Writing and reviewing it are important group tasks. 3. The speechwriter must have access to the speaker. 4. Presentation of the speech should be rehearsed to assure that it will have the desired impact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure clear timeline, assigned roles, access to speaker, and rehearsal sessions before finalizing a speech.

rubrics_metrics.name: Speaking carries credibility and allows mid-course corrections
rubrics_metrics.description: While a written message is somewhat impersonal, the spoken word carries the credibility of the speaker. The speaking situation is flexible and can be altered to fit the response of the audience; in a speaking situation you can make mid-course corrections.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use speaking to leverage personal credibility and real-time interaction; prepare speakers to read audience cues and adapt accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consistency with organizational messages
rubrics_metrics.description: The speech must be consistent with other messages disseminated by the organization. The speaker must be familiar with positions taken in written communication, and must strive to articulate them in a personal style that is consistent with the view of the organization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Align speech content and tone with existing organizational communications to avoid mixed messages; brief speaker on organizational positions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Set realistic objectives for spoken communication
rubrics_metrics.description: For most techniques we cautioned you to limit your objectives to communication and sometimes retention. When messages are spoken skillfully, however, sometimes you can expect to achieve acceptance of the message, formation or change of an attitude, and even behavior. Even with face-to-face communication you won't be able to attain attitudinal and behavioral objectives as often as cognitive objectives, but you will be able to attain them more often than with other forms of communication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plan for cognitive outcomes primarily; consider speaking when aiming for higher likelihood of attitude or behavior change, but remain realistic about probabilities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose speaking when two-way interaction is needed
rubrics_metrics.description: Speaking allows more two-way communicating than writing and leads to different effects. Speaking skills are especially useful in the symmetric model because more feedback is possible when the speaker and audience meet face to face.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use speeches, dialogues, and face-to-face meetings when feedback, negotiation, or listening to publics is a program objective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tailor length and technicality to audience involvement
rubrics_metrics.description: Low-involvement publics will listen to someone speak if the presentation is entertaining, brief, and not too technical. Aware and active high-involvement publics can tolerate longer, less dramatic, and more technical speeches or discussions. They want the information. They listen carefully.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess audience involvement level and adjust content complexity and duration accordingly; be brief and engaging for low-involvement audiences, thorough and technical for high-involvement audiences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cost and time budgeting for speeches
rubrics_metrics.description: Spoken communication doesn't cost a lot of money compared to electronic media and brochures, but preparation of spoken messages can take considerable time. Most expense comes from hiring speechwriters. Time budgeting techniques are especially useful in planning spoken communication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allocate time for research, writing, review, rehearsals and coaching; budget for professional speechwriting and training where necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measures for evaluating speeches
rubrics_metrics.description: To measure whether communication took place, you might: count the number of people who hear the speech; review content of press clippings resulting from the meeting; keep track of kinds of people who attend; record the number of times you articulate the view of a public to your management. To measure cognitive, attitudinal, and behavioral effects, administer a questionnaire right after the speech, mail it out later, or ask in a telephone interview. If unable to use a questionnaire, take informal measurement by circulating and listening to audience reaction. For press sessions, code articles to indicate whether the writer attached a positive, negative, or neutral evaluation to what the speaker said.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use both quantitative (attendance counts, clippings, coding) and qualitative (surveys, informal interviews, observation) methods; administer evaluations promptly; include measures of management uptake.

rubrics_metrics.name: Research thoroughly before writing
rubrics_metrics.description: Statements made about the topic should be reviewed in order to know what the main arguments are and what raw data are available. In addition to books and periodicals, check professional or trade journals and government publications for statistics and informed opinions. Your own files are also important: be able to put your hands quickly on everything your organization’s managers have written or said on the topic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Perform library and file research, consult trade and government sources to assemble credible supporting data before outlining the speech.

rubrics_metrics.name: Define the 'Big Idea' in one line
rubrics_metrics.description: After you've gathered the data, but before you prepare an outline, the all-important question is, What is the main point we want to make with this speech? The speechwriter should be able to summarize the big idea of the speech in a single line.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Craft a single-line central thesis to keep the speech focused; use it to weed out interesting but irrelevant information.

rubrics_metrics.name: Organize with classical outline
rubrics_metrics.description: A good speech has an introduction, a body, and a conclusion. If a one-page outline—with the classical I, A., 1. a. format for arranging main and subordinate points—is submitted to the speaker for discussion and refinement beforehand, the writing task will be easier, and fewer alterations will have to be made on the completed script.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prepare a concise one-page classical outline and review it with the speaker prior to full scripting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Work closely with the speaker
rubrics_metrics.description: The speechwriter must work with the speaker on every phase of developing the speech. The word choices, even the length and rhythm of the sentences, must be appropriate to the individual speaking style. The speaker must feel familiar enough with the supporting data to field questions and defend his or her views. Ideally, the writer should have worked in close conjunction with the speaker; if not, the writer must have access to the speaker and at least one session in which the writer hears the script read by the speaker.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tailor wording and rhythm to speaker's style, ensure speaker familiarity with facts, schedule read-throughs and revisions with the speaker to build trust and fit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Introduction: choose appropriate opening
rubrics_metrics.description: The rule of thumb concerning a joke is threefold: the speaker can deliver it effectively; it flows out of the experience of the speaker; it is appropriate to the subject. If those tests can be met, a moment of levity is effective. If it falls flat in rehearsal, or the speaker wants to open with something accurate that is appropriate to the moment, then the humorous story is best left out. If the speech is to be serious in tone, an ominous opening statement might be appropriate. Intriguing little-known facts or revealing bits of personal history can raise curiosity and put the speaker at ease.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select openings (joke, anecdote, startling fact, ominous statement) that the speaker can deliver authentically and that suit the occasion; always rehearse openings and be prepared to drop elements that don't work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plan time allocation and Q&A
rubrics_metrics.description: No one will get mad at a speaker who made a twenty-minute speech when he was scheduled for twenty-five minutes. If you've narrowed your topic sufficiently, you can be complete and still be brief. If you’ve been commissioned to fill an hour, why not plan to devote half of it to fielding questions?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be conservative on length, respect audience tolerance, and allocate substantial time for questions when appropriate (e.g., half the time for an hour session).

rubrics_metrics.name: Research audience composition before delivery
rubrics_metrics.description: Research the composition of the audience in order to advise the speaker who the listeners are, what their interest level is, what they already know about the subject, and what kinds of questions they are likely to ask.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Before coaching/delivery, profile the audience to advise tone, detail level, and anticipated Q&A topics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide coaching and rehearsal, use videotape consultants
rubrics_metrics.description: Some executives welcome coaching and preparation. Others are insulted to think they must be rehearsed and trained in order to perform adequately. It may be advisable... to make it official management policy that all speakers undergo a 'prep session.' Professional speech consultants, using videotape, are available to conduct such training.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Institutionalize prep sessions and use videotaped coaching to improve delivery; adapt approach to individual receptivity but insist on rehearsal.
